title: Compensating differential

definition.text: The extra pay a worker must be offered to take an unpleasant or risky job instead of other jobs they could do.

facts.text: For an especially pleasant job the differential is negative: workers accept lower pay.
The idea, credited to Adam Smith, has been used to study injury risk, the money value workers put on their own lives, and wage gaps between regions.
Economists usually expect wages to be lower in places with high levels of amenity, so wage gaps can reveal how much an area's attractiveness is worth.
A hedonic wage function plots how wages rise with a job's undesirable features, such as the probability of injury.

notes: Not the same as compensating variation (S:9fc5350430fd), which the page distinguishes.

definition.text: A survey-based statistical technique, mainly from market research, that works out how much people value each attribute that makes up a product or service.

facts.text: Respondents see a controlled set of products broken down by attribute, and their choices reveal the implicit value, or part-worth, of each attribute.
Marketing professor Paul E. Green developed it, and Jordan Louviere pioneered the choice-based version that underlies discrete choice analysis.
It is also called discrete choice modelling or stated preference research.
Because the number of attribute combinations grows exponentially, fractional factorial designs cut the profiles respondents must judge.

title: Best–worst scaling

definition.text: A survey method in which respondents pick the best and worst items from repeated subsets of a list, invented by Jordan Louviere in 1987.

facts.text: Choice frequencies are analysed with a random utility model to estimate how much each item is preferred.
It is closely related to conjoint analysis and discrete choice experiments and has been adopted in health, transport and environmental economics.
It shares the disadvantages of all stated preference techniques.
